A receptionist is a person whose job is to be the first point of contact for visitors, clients, or callers at an organization. Think of them as the "face" and "voice" of a place — the first person you see when you walk into an office, a hotel, a hospital, or a clinic, and the first voice you hear when you call one of those places.

The word comes from the idea of receiving people — welcoming them in, acknowledging them, and directing them where they need to go.

A receptionist's work revolves around managing the flow of people and communication into an organization. Their typical responsibilities include:

  • Greeting visitors — When someone walks in, the receptionist welcomes them, asks for their name and purpose, and lets the relevant person inside know they have arrived.
  • Answering phone calls — They handle incoming calls, take messages, and transfer calls to the right department or person.
  • Scheduling appointments — In many places like clinics or salons, the receptionist manages a diary or calendar, booking and confirming appointments for clients.
  • Handling enquiries — People often approach the receptionist with questions. The receptionist either answers them directly or guides them to someone who can.
  • Administrative tasks — This can include sorting mail, managing files, responding to emails, and keeping the front desk area organized.

The exact duties vary from one workplace to another, but the common thread is always the same: receive people and communication, and manage them efficiently.

Receptionists are found in almost every kind of organization that regularly deals with the public or clients:

  • Hospitals and clinics — A medical receptionist registers patients, collects their details, and schedules their appointments with doctors.
  • Hotels — A hotel receptionist (sometimes called "front desk staff") checks guests in and out, assigns rooms, and handles requests during a guest's stay.
  • Corporate offices — A receptionist manages visitors, handles calls, and often controls who is allowed entry into the building.
  • Schools and universities — They assist students, parents, and staff at the administrative front desk.
  • Salons, spas, and gyms — They book sessions, handle payments, and welcome clients.
  • Law firms, accounting firms, and other professional offices — They manage client arrivals and maintain a professional, organized front desk.

A receptionist holds a position of great importance, even though it might not always seem that way at first. Consider this: the receptionist is the very first impression a visitor gets of an entire organization. If a receptionist is warm, efficient, and helpful, a visitor feels at ease and thinks well of the place. If the receptionist is rude or disorganized, the visitor's opinion of the entire organization is damaged — even before they've spoken to anyone else.

This is why the role demands a particular combination of skills: good communication, a calm and pleasant manner, the ability to multitask, and professionalism under pressure.

It helps to understand how a receptionist differs from roles that sound similar:

  • A secretary or personal assistant (PA) typically works closely with one specific person — like a manager or executive — handling their schedule, correspondence, and tasks. A receptionist, by contrast, serves the organization as a whole and interacts with everyone — visitors, callers, and all staff.
  • A customer service representative usually handles issues or complaints, often over the phone or online. A receptionist's focus is primarily on being the first point of contact and directing people, not resolving complex service issues.
  • A clerk handles specific administrative or clerical tasks (like data entry or filing) and may not be positioned at the front of an organization dealing with walk-in visitors.

That said, in smaller organizations, one person might carry out all of these roles at once.

"Receptionist" is a standard, formal word used comfortably in both spoken and written English. It is completely neutral — it can refer to a man or a woman without any change to the word itself.

You might see it used in job postings ("We are hiring a receptionist"), in conversation ("Let me check with the receptionist"), or in descriptions of a workplace ("The receptionist directed me to the third floor").

1. The receptionist at the dental clinic reminded me of my appointment by calling the day before.
  2. When I arrived at the law firm, the receptionist asked me to sign the visitor's register and offered me a seat.
  3. She works as a receptionist at a five-star hotel, which means she often assists guests from all over the world.
  4. The company is looking for a receptionist who is fluent in both English and Hindi.
  5. I called the hospital, but the receptionist put me on hold for ten minutes.
  6. He was polite and well-dressed — just what you'd expect from a receptionist at a high-end corporate office.

A receptionist is a professional who sits at the front desk of an organization, welcoming visitors, answering phones, scheduling appointments, and handling general enquiries. They are the first point of contact between the outside world and the organization, making their role both visible and vital. Whether in a hospital, a hotel, a school, or a corporate office, the receptionist ensures that people and communication are received smoothly, directed correctly, and handled with care.
